Or I can rephrase the question: Of those who have been replaced and removed from their positions, is there a single one who is not a Croat or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this situation very well. This is a period in which Croatian children did not even go to school in Mostar but went to Zapana, Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You really ought to answer the questions and not engage upon widespread explanations, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, but the impression gained will be a mistaken one, because all the directors are Muslims but it is fact that no Muslim children were in Mostar -- no Croat children were in Mostar at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, was anyone appointed without being a Croat [as interpreted], a council sit?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a situation at that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And all the appointments were of Muslims, right?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe Cupina, that he found these facts in some references, in some sources that he referred to. So that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Will the registrar show us 5D 01091. Mr. Smajkic, while we are waiting for this document, you will recall these events. This is a document from the 19th of April, 1992, and if the registrar would scroll it down, this is an order by General Perisic. We have seen it here and in other courtrooms as well about the artillery attack, an artillery attack on parts of the city. Do we agree, Mr. Smajkic, that Cim, Ilici, Bijeli Brijeg, and Donja Mahala, parts of the city of Mostar, are not military targets but civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are sections of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Will the registrar please scroll the document up. We want to see the heading. Mr. Smajkic, this was 10 -- 10 days prior to the transference of powers for the defence to the HVO. So at this moment, the actual power in the city was vested in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, still.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. 5D 01112 is the next document that we would kindly ask the registrar to show us. This is -- and can we see the next page immediately. Again, an excerpt from the book that you revised [as interpreted], that is the book of Mr. Cupina. And if we take a look at the first and second paragraphs, you will see, Mr. Smajkic, that there was a quite pronounced dissatisfaction with the activities of the civilian authorities; i.e., the activities of the Crisis Staff. And then in the third paragraph, which starts in this way: "Precisely on account of such inadequate activity, the --" and so on and so forth -- "the activists of the Patriotic League had to set up their own Crisis Staff." Is this what it says, Mr. Smajkic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So in addition to the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Mostar, which was its official designation, there obviously also existed a Crisis Staff of the Patriotic League; right?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Because the people who were members of that Crisis Staff are indicated here, I have no doubt that you know all these people.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can conclude on the basis of these names that this was not a political body but people who were actually preparing themselves for the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting anything otherwise. I just want us to agree and for you to confirm, if you can, that the Patriotic League in Mostar formed a separate Crisis Staff. At the bottom of this same page - and will the registrar please scroll the page down - we can see a reference being made to the fact that already on the 10th of February, 1991, in Bihac the president of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, proclaimed the existence of the Patriotic League for B and H. Obviously this Patriotic League in Mostar was a component part of this Patriotic League for the B and H which Alija Izetbegovic proclaimed as existing on the 10th of February, 1991.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what the programme of the Patriotic League was? What did it advocate?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have its programme at that time, and I was not that much involved in this subject matter, the subject matter of defence, in this initial stage, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: But do you know in view of the numerous articles and books that were published on this subject, including this one which you revised [as interpreted], what the programme of the Patriotic League was? Was it set up to defend all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina or just to defend the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the authorship actually hails from the idea of Alija Izetbegovic, it could by no means be just for the protection of the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You are convinced of that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief a few days ago, you commented on this and reverted to the subject today, namely developments in respect of Boban -- the Boban-Karadzic meeting in Graz. Did you or did you not discuss that already?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I did not even know nor had read about it, but I said how it had been, and I stand behind that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, in 1991 -- in mid-1991, did you have any information, did you know anything about the secret Muslim-Serbian negotiations and talks?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me too much. You're asking -- that is a tall order. This is a feel that is alien to me. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that after they had been busted, so to speak -- I mean after they found out that these talks had indeed taken place -- did the papers throughout the then former Yugoslavia extensively write about that and that the memoirs of these developments were written by the participants of at least from the Muslim side, which is Muhamed Filipovic, Zulfikarpasic and Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed about it in a way, but I had no direct insight into the happenings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: But did you -- you do know that there was some secret Muslim-Serb negotiations held in mid-1992?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see from the papers, such talks were indeed conducted in order for the former Yugoslavia to part, the nations of the former Yugoslavia to part in a peaceful way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. I'm just asking you whether you know about it or not, knew about it.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could read about it in the papers. I don't know about the actual substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All right. We have already referred to the 29th of April, 1992, namely, the moment when the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Mostar transferred the powers for the defence to the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Will the registrar please show us document 5D 01093. And whilst we are waiting Mr. Smajkic, yesterday one of the members of that Crisis Staff was with us here yesterday, and he told us that all the activities of the staff ended on the 15th of May, 1992, and under a decision of the HVO Mostar, that Crisis Staff was disbanded on that date. I would like show you in that connection a document which on precisely that date that refers to precisely that Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly. We did not manage to decipher the signatory's name but it impresses the commander of the 1st Mostar Battalion and refers to the coordination of the quartermaster service and the needs to inform the Crisis Staff of the TO of that. So Mr. Smajkic, a while ago we saw that the Patriotic League, according to Mr. Cupina, that is, had set up a separate Crisis Staff in Mostar distinct from this Municipal Assembly of Mostar Crisis Staff. Now we see here the Crisis Staff of the TO. As you were part of the developments and the organisation there then -- in fact, a few days ago you said that you lobbied with Mr. Izetbegovic for the replacement of Mr. Hadziosmanovic, and that you personally informed via Radio Mostar about his replacement, do you perhaps know what Crisis Staff of the TO this was?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When answering Mr. Scott's questions, you mentioned how Mr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic was elected, Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic, he was elected as the leader of the SDA in Mostar or, rather, as president of the regional SDA in Herzegovina. And on that occasion you said that the main argument in his favour was that his brother Mustafa was a member of the Young Muslims. Page 73 and 74 of the unofficial version of the transcript. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I still believe that that's how it worked. That's my assessment. You asked me about it, that was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. You certainly know and you can certainly answer my question as to whether Alija Izetbegovic was a member of the Young Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic is not the only person whose political career prospered because he was a member of the Young Muslims. You probably know something about the SDA and its establishment and I therefore assume you would agree that one of the founders of the SDA -- or, rather, that members of the Young Muslims were some of the most prominent founders. For the sake of the transcript, it was Teufik Velagic, Omer Behmen, Alija Izetbegovic. I'll repeat the names: Teufik Velagic, Omer Behmen, et cetera. Were they at the very top of the SDA from the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Later they were promoted to positions at the state level. Omer Behmen became the BH ambassador in Iran; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Mohamed Sacirbegovic was the person who was promoted to the highest ranking position. He was the ambassador of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the United Nations in New York, and later he was the minister of foreign affairs. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I can see that you know what I'm going to ask you about. His father Nedzib was also a member of the Young Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So we can see that Mr. Izetbegovic pursued policies that attached significant importance to whether or not someone had been a member of the Young Muslims. What kind of an organisation were the Young Muslims? That's an important question. I have Sef Turhoj's [phoen] book on the Young Muslims, or entitled "The Young Muslims." Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: It's a collection of documents produced by that movement, and it was also based on some conversations with surviving witnesses. The only original part of the book is the introduction. Could the registrar please show us 5D 01082. Could this document please be put on the screen. While we're waiting for it to appear on the screen, Mr. Smajkic, this document concerns a conversation with Alija Izetbegovic, and this conversation was published in the book. Could we have a look at the next page, please. We can see the young Mr. Izetbegovic here, and let's have a look the next page, please. Mr. Izetbegovic says how the organisation was founded, and he explains its objectives, and then from the middle onwards he says: "I remember that one of the items mentioned the unity of the Muslims throughout the world. I think that was item 4. And item 5 read as follows: 'The practical achievement of Islam.' And there was a secretive formula there. There was no comment. It says we always interpreted this as being tantamount to the creation of a very large Muslim state. For us, that is what this item in fact meant whereas all the other items also had an explanation accompanying the principle, or a lengthy or brief explanation, whereas all that was stated here is the practical information of Islam, and then there is no comment." Can we have a look at the next page, please. At the top the author of the book asks Mr. Izetbegovic, Did this, among other things, mean that there was a request for certain discipline, subordination? He answered yes. I also interpreted item 5 in this way. "We didn't comment this item because we believed that it was a certain conspiratorial item, a secret. It represented something that should not be said at that time. I always interpreted this item as a request for a sort of political implementation of Islam." Is that what it says in this book, Mr. Smajkic? And it was published, as we could see on page 1, in 1992, when Mr. Izetbegovic was politically extremely powerful. Is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Could the registry show us 5D 01083. This document is from the same book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I've been quiet this afternoon but I'm just wondering how much this assists us. All we're doing now is reading excerpts of material and then the question to the witness is just -- look at line 23 of page 96: "Does the page that I've just shown you say that?" And the witness says, "That's what it says." Now, how much does it really assist the Chamber to simply go through a series of documents and ask the witness if that's what it says?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but as a general rule, Mr. Jonjic concludes such a series of questions by putting a question of a general nature to the witness, a question of a general nature that -- that resumes or synthesises all the other questions, and this then helps the Chamber. But as you have said, at the moment we can't see what the purpose of these questions is but we are anticipating or we are waiting for the question that will clarify everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. What is at stake here is the ideological background of the president -- of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is one of the elements of his staff policies, and I think that Mr. Smajkic is in a good position to explain to us whether these statements are in accordance with Islam. Could we have a look at the document 5D 01083, and very briefly we will have a look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: It's an oath of -- taken by members of the Young Muslims. This is an organisation that Mr. Izetbegovic belonged to, and he recruited his most reliable staff members from this organisation. Mr. Smajkic, if you can just read through it very quickly. Have a look at this oath which mentions unconditional sacrifice for Islam, for the greatness of Islam and for the benefits of all the Muslims throughout the world. Mr. Smajkic, would you agree that there's nothing specifically Bosnian here? Such an oath could have been taken in, for example, Saudi Arabia, Iran, Indonesia; in any country inhabited by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this before, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: But is there anything that is specifically Bosnian in this document?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this represents the religious enthusiasm of people who were very young at the time and who dreamt of being free to practice their own religion. It doesn't really have anything to do with statehood.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Could we have a look at the following document, 5D 01084. And this document is part of the testimony of a member of the Young Muslims, and it says that in a multi-ethnic and multi-confessional area, such as Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to the ideas of this group, it mentions how the problems of Croats and Serbs could be dealt with. Could we have a look at the following page, please, and this is the last excerpt that we will be looking at from this book. If we have a look at the middle of the document. Scroll down a little more. That's fine. In response to a question put by the Chamber with regard to the purposes of the organisation, and in order to save time, I'll summarise what it says. A member of the organisation responded that at an appropriate point in time they wanted to establish an independent Bosnia that would become part of an Islam state, and all the parts of Yugoslavia inhabited by Muslims would be part of that state, they would take power into their own hands. What would they do with the Serbs and the Croats? We'd be tolerant with regard to Serbs and Croats. And how would Turks, Serbs, and Bulgarians join this state? The answer was, We would move them out or solve the problem in some other way. Mr. Smajkic, I am not asking you to confirm such a position but all I want to know is whether you can confirm that a member of this organisation actually said this.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what we can read in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's now go back to the purpose of the exercise. We're trying to demonstrate the reasons that Izetbegovic had when pursuing party policies and state policies in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can we have a look at another excerpt from another book. 5D 01081 is the number of that document. While waiting for it to appear on the screen, Mr. Smajkic, your name is Enver -- you're certainly familiar with the name Enver Redzic.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: He is an academic, a member of the Academy of Bosnia-Herzegovina and certainly one of the most prominent Muslim intellectuals, certainly one of the most prominent historians; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So this is a book of his, entitled "A Hundred Years of Muslim Policies," in which he comments on the Islamic Declaration. Could we have a look at the next page, please. The Islamic Declaration, Mr. Smajkic, you will agree with me, I think, the Islamic Declaration is one of Mr. Izetbegovic's most important texts, and he was put on trial in Sarajevo for this text in '83.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: He never rejected his positions in the Islamic Declaration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Have you read that book of his?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm waiting for the interpretation. If you have read that book, then you're able to see how Mr. Redzic analysed the book. He was a regular member of the Academy of Arts and Science in Bosnia-Herzegovina and he is a Muslim; isn't that correct? Given that this is an article about 40 pages long, I've only selected certain parts of the text. We don't have time to go through everything. I think we can have a look at the next page, though. And the next one. That's the one. Have a look at the middle part of the document, in which analysis is made of the Islamic Declaration and the Redzic says that any discussion of the national issue of Bosnian Muslims is not included in the declaration. It -- when analysed, this declaration doesn't touch on the name of the Muslims, although there were a lot of discussions of that during that period. The declaration completely neglects the question of national identity. Could we have a look at the next page, please. In the middle, the last sentence in the middle of this paragraph, the one that hasn't been crossed out, it says that Izetbegovic's thesis is that the Muslim doesn't exist as an entity, not as an individual, but as a collective entity. Then let's have a look at the last page, please. At the very bottom. I'll read it through to save time. "To be ideologically unilateral means to be intolerant. The protagonists of Islam are not immune to this. The position that Islam is not just a religion and that means an ideology is a position that Izetbegovic emphasises with the conclusion on Islam and non-Islamic systems not being reconcilable." And then there's another quotation from Mr. Izetbegovic's declaration: "There is no peace or co-existence between the Islam faith and non-Islamic social and political institutions. Islam excludes the possibility and the right of any kind of ideology being operational in its territory." Mr. Smajkic, could you briefly comment on these positions of one of the most prominent Islam scientists or academics.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honours, I can comment on this very superficially right now, but I would simply like to inform you that Mr. Izetbegovic was a thinker and that he thought through philosophical questions, historical questions, questions that concerned the history of civilisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: In order to come to such conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, but he couldn't discuss certain issues because each of these articles in the system that existed at the time was written under a pseudonym. So he couldn't have dealt with issues that concerned nationality or relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw a while ago an illustration of the activity of Izetbegovic's authentic organisation, the original organisation, the Young Muslims, and now we saw his Islamic Declaration. There is a continuity between the two, don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd refrain from commenting on that. You have said quite a lot to me, and I would have to give it some thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But you did say that the Islamic Declaration of Alija Izetbegovic was a consequence of his thinking endeavours. So I would like to say that in thinking Islam through in this way, which Enver Redzic designates as being intolerant, exclusive, and totalitarian, that he did not just stick to the doctrine, the theoretical level, but as you can see and as yourself confirmed in actually appointing the -- his key associates, he bore in mind the fact that they should actually hail from the same ideological milieus. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that can be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I shall ask you just a couple of questions so that I leave enough time for Mr. Coric and for General Praljak. Will the registrar show us 5D 01069, please. That document, of course. While we're waiting for the document, Mr. Smajkic, your calling is primarily of a spiritual nature, so it would be only logical for you to predominantly not dedicate yourself to lay matters, specifically not to defence; right?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: This document that we see in front us is a document sent by the police administration of Mostar to different HVO bodies -- no, rather to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, I apologise, and attached to it is a record or minutes of meeting. Let us take a short look at the first page and then take a longer look at the second page, please. The heading says the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- no, no, no. The next page, please. Can we have the next page, please. So this document says at the top of the page Independent Unit Muslim forces of Mostar. It refers to some persons that you also yourself referred to during the examination-in-chief. If I remember correctly, you did mention Mr. Custovic. However, on the second page -- will the registrar please show us the next-to-last page of this document, please. So I shall read again to save time: "Attached to this letter is also a list of personnel, members of the unit of the Muslim forces of Mostar on the 21st of November, 1992. By their signatures, the commission guarantees that the situation as indicated is correct and full moral and material responsibility. Any things that might remain unclear shall be explained by the stated commission together, I, with the presence of the Mostar mufti, at the joint meeting with representatives of the Islamic centre at the headquarters of the Muslim forces in Zenica, with the supreme Emir of the Muslim forces and other members of the Sure at the helm." Is this what it says, Mr. Smajkic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember these developments, this meeting in Zenica and the compiling of this list? So this is the end of November 1992.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states that it is in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but with the presence of the Mostar mufti.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But where? Where does it say with the presence of the Mostar mufti?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All -- "Anything unclear will be clarified by the mentioned commission together with the presence of the Mostar mufti, at a joint meeting, it shall be explained --"

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shall be explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But did you participate in that? This is just a compilation of a list of members. Nothing is problematic there.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot retain everything in memory, but when you referred to this person indicated here, this was some sort of an agreement. A person was sent, a person whose name is Ibrahim Mimic, and possibly appeared in the capacity of Emir. This is what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: But you did participate in this compilation of the list and you coordinated matters with this Muslim centre in Zenica. Did you or did you not? I would not like to dwell too much on this.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not avoiding anything, it's just that I need to recall some things. I did participate in parts of this activity because I -- we were supposed to coordinate matters along some coordination lines because these are people from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the headquarters of the Muslim forces was in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They thought themselves to be that, but as you can see, these are -- we have documents with such-and-such signatories and these or those units, but this was not coordinated in a way that you could say that they were thus organised in the command sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Okay. But confirm this for me: The "Instructions for the Muslim Fighter" were also published and printed in Zenica; right?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can we just see another two documents? I would like to ask the registrar -- I hope that I shall have enough time. 5D 01115, 1115 is the first one, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to go back to the preceding document, document number 69. On the -- in the list of weapons -- can we see the document? Can we have a look at the document on the screen? In English it's entitled "Record."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 01069. That is the covering letter. Then the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page. There it is. Sir, could you have a look at the last line. There's something missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right, Your Honour. There is something missing in the electronic version which does appear in the -- in the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could place it on the ELMO, perhaps. Digital versions aren't perfect. Far from it. We will have a look at the document on the ELMO now. Have a look at the last line. Could you read out the last line, Witness. What does it say? [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here 1 piece of automatic rifle issued to the Mostar mufti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you explain the fact that a member of the clergy receives a weapon or can receive a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, simply speaking, I never used anything of the kind, but I was indeed once issued with one. It was a state of war. And you could see that all the political representatives all had been issued with similar items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I was wondering about. You were at war, but what about the other members of the clergy in Mostar? The Catholic bishop, for example, or the Orthodox priest? Were they also issued with weapons? Did they have weapons too? Why did you have a weapon and the others did not? How would you explain the fact that you personally had a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I explained this by the fact that it was war and that every person had to be armed whether they used the weapons or not, whether they were in units or not. I had it at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But is it normal in your religion that members of the clergy have arms, have weapons in their possession? Is this provided for in the Koran?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, one had to exercise caution. It is not provided for in the Koran, but as in moving about we were exposed to the danger of being attacked, and as we were responsible people, we had to take care of our own protection on our own initiative, because we had no guards and there was no one else there to defend us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I meant to leave this for the end, but while we are at the subject, I will continue to pursue this line that you have initiated, but I will ask this in the form of a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, did you use -- do you use for personal protection a pistol or an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never used either. It was there and could be had, and I had it at my disposal, but I never used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I shall refrain from asking Mr. Smajkic some other things which I had meant to ask him. I shall just show him a document which I believe complements what Colleague Alaburic talked about today. Can we see 5D 01115. 1115. This is a document which describes the situation in Mostar on the 28th of May, 1993. Do you agree, Mr. Smajkic, that this is a document of the 3rd Brigade of the HVO of the 28th of May, and that that was 19 days after the outbreak or, rather, the escalation of the conflict between the Muslim and the Croat forces in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you. Will the registrar please scroll the document up so that we can see the content. The commander of the 3rd Brigade commands that an analysis be undertaken of the attitude and conduct of members of the Muslim nation who found themselves in the units, and then he goes on to ask how many Muslims crossed over to the side of the army of BH with weapons or without weapons, how many Muslims had left their units and how many remained in the units. And then it goes on to -- can we scroll the document a bit further up, please. He then enjoins upon the information and propaganda service, the IPD, information and propaganda activity service in the HVO, to make the work more efficient, to intensify the work in order to unmask the intentions of the extreme sections of the army of BH and the part of the Muslim leadership and people. It also stresses the necessity of further co-existence in the field, in the terrain in which the unit is, and the necessity to render operational the organs of authority on the basis of the UN plan. And the last item is to retain members of the Muslim nationality in the units, namely those who are not -- namely those who are not extremists and only promote a joint struggle against a joint enemy. Is this what it says, Mr. Smajkic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That is what it says in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So some 20 days after the outbreak of the conflict, the brigade of the HVO headquartered in Mostar speaks about the necessity of further joint life, joint cooperation, joint fighting against the common enemy; right?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what it says here, but what they did in the field, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: All right. Just another question, because I have gone over my time limit. A few days ago you mentioned -- that was page 132, line 9 and 10, of the unofficial record, asked whom -- whom of the accused you knew, you mentioned Mr. Valentin Coric. Tell me, when did you meet Mr. Valentin Coric?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was during the post-war establishment of the organs of authority in the cantons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And when was this specifically? What position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the minister of the interior of the canton.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you have meetings with him frequently? Did you cooperate with him?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, but I knew him and I know him through his deputy, but I did not have dealings with him specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You are referring to Mr. Dzihic as his deputy?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You are talking about the establishment of a joint police force; right?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's a well-known person, both in the Assembly of the canton and through other forms of activities and contacts and his presence to some joint events, but otherwise I didn't have direct dealings and talks with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have another 15 minutes before the break. Mr. Coric has 15 minutes for his questions, we will then have our break, and then Mr. Praljak will have another 15 minutes. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examination by the accused Coric:

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Smajkic.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: My name is Valentin Coric, I am one of the accused. I'd like to put a number of questions to you that concern the political situation in Mostar when a conflict broke out in the Muslim Corps. There was a replacement of the legally elected president of the SDA in Mostar who was also the president of the SDA of the town of Mostar. A certain circle of which you were a part requested that he be replaced. You admitted that.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I've had a look at the names of the people involved in that circle and I notice there are quite a few people who didn't participate in the first democratically held elections; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't know who participated in the first elections, but I do know the people from that circle who were in my vicinity at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about the Council of Muslims of Herzegovina, we're talking about the declaration, the charter, we're talking about the people who took part in the drafting of those three documents and who took part in those institutions?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know those people well but I don't know anything about 1991. I don't know whether they participated or not in that, though, in the elections. That's what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I find this a little odd. Why was it legitimate for these people to participate in political battles?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were forced to act in that way because Mr. Hadziosmanovic wouldn't take into consideration the interests of the Bosniak people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Who forced them?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean who forced them? These people became aware of the situation, and they found methods and means of becoming active. They were trying to find a way that would enable them to solve the problems of education, the judiciary, of humanitarian aid, of protection in the most effective way. And Mr. Hadziosmanovic didn't act in the way he should have acted in that respect, so naturally people were quite right in raising this issue, the issue of his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: That's my question. Were these people entitled to bring into question the position of a legally elected person?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't act in secret. We had the right to say that we weren't satisfied with such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I obviously can't obtain a realistic answer from you, so my following question is: That was the conclusion of a group of individuals. They decided that he wasn't working correctly. You also referred to the people, and you also said there was a small part of the people who were with the SDA president.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said and I believe that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did you establish a political party since you were not previously engaged in a political party? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never a member of a political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I know that, but I know that people surrounding you were. I wanted to know what the results were -- what results they obtained when they participated in the first democratic elections. It's odd that you don't know anything about this. I'd like to move on, I don't want to waste any time since time is precious. The conclusion one can draw is that you received instructions from someone to replace such a person. You weren't supported by the people. Did you receive instructions from the outside?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those instructions came from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: How, or was there a referendum held?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but there was disagreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to present some arguments to you. At the time, there was a significant number of Bosniaks or Muslims in the HVO. As we have already seen today, that was the case. School directors were Bosniaks; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the first stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: That's the period I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first stage -- well, Ms. Nozica had a list from the first government, and it included Muslim ministers. They were replaced within one month, and that's what the HVO and the HVO government did. A few months later, there were new people who were appointed whereas the others were replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the SDA, I'm talking about the policies and political positions in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was then going to compare things. But what I want to clarify before this Chamber is what the real cause of the conflict between the Croats and Bosniaks in Mostar was. My question is as follows: Would you agree that the lines facing the Serbo-Chetniks had already been established after June, 1993, and those lines didn't move almost until the end of the war? Would you agree with that? At that time the Croats and Bosniaks fought together. They were in the HVO and acted within the HVO in a joint manner. And let me remind you that the HVO was a legal member of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So would you also agree with what I said in my previous question?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with that because, as I have said, there was some secret war being waged from the very beginning and there had been lines established at Podvelezje. There were joint units there, and they drove away the Serbo-Chetnik aggressor there. When the Croatian forces remained to guard those lines, the Serbs took them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You are wasting my time, but I'd just like to repeat something that's already been said here. We're talking about the period when the relationship between the HVO and Independent Battalion or the ABiH was 9 to 1. There would be 9 HVO soldiers and 1 member of the Independent Battalion. At that time they established lines facing the Serbs; is that correct, during that period?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And what happened afterwards? Would you agree that the armed forces in Herzegovina that were part of the ABiH were strengthened? There was no imminent war with the Croats. At least, the Croats weren't expecting such a war. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The forces were strengthened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: My question is why? There was no longer a war with the Serbs and it was certain that we wouldn't be fighting the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That couldn't have been certain, because the politicians were drawing up maps and trying to reach agreements and no one knew what was going to happen. The Croats and Croatian leadership developed an appetite for the territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You're wasting my time again.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Today we had a look at documents that mentioned the arming of the members of the Independent Battalion. Do you believe that these weapons could have come from some other country apart from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the whole they came from Croatia. There were independent channels that were used. Certain arms were bought from Chetniks, et cetera, but on the whole that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You said that you knew some of our common friends; isn't that correct? And do you know who I'm -- who I bear in mind?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Dziho?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Among others.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Cupina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. So you've spoken to them and they know how the first stage of arming proceeded. Remember the late Daidza?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that at the time we were very close to each other? Do you agree that we trusted each other, at least, if we weren't close?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so. I don't know what your personal relationships were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about intimate personal relationships.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were -- they were friendly relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to conclude now. I have a few more questions. After all those conflicts in Herzegovina or in the area for which you are competent as a mufti, could you confirm the following: The Croats -- I'll start with the top -- were expelled from Travnik, Kakanj, Vares, Bugojno, Konjic, Jablanica, Eastern Mostar. Maybe I've forgotten something, but that's sufficient. Do you know how many Croats were in fact expelled or, rather, do you know how many Croats left?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's true that they left, that they weren't expelled, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a different matter. I have different arguments.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also have different arguments. But they did leave. They weren't expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I've read an article in the Sarajevo newspaper which says that of those Croats that were expelled at the time, only about 15 per cent of those Croats have returned to their homes. Are you aware of that? I'm talking about Kakanj, Vares, Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was probably a small percentage, but that's the percentage when it comes to all the various ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know at the same time in Herzegovina in Capljina and in Stolac in Southern Mostar and Western Mostar - and I'm talking about the Bosniaks - do you know that, according to that article, about 85 per cent of the Bosniaks have returned to their homes?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably in the area of Stolac and Capljina. In Mostar, that's not the case, because they wouldn't allow this in the western part because of obstructions to returning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Since I've worked in the police, would you agree that while I was the minister in the canton in Eastern Mostar, there were only 54 Croat inhabitants, and that's in the entire area under the control of the Bosniak authorities?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number but it's a small number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You know it's a small number.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Western Mostar at the same time there were about 8 to 10.000 Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several thousand, but I don't think there are that many. We don't have the statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Several thousand; 8.000, 6.000?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a large number. 5 or 6.000, perhaps. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So we do agree that there were at least 5 or 6.000 inhabitants there.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But could we also agree that 30 individuals were killed when people attempted to return to Western Mostar, and that's from 1995 until five years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I have enough information about people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I'm talking about that, because I know you were in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I was in the police for seven years.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I have to say that not a single case was dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: That's not correct, but I'm not being examined, you are. You have all the information on the MUP according to which investigations were carried out.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single individual was charged and processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: That's your claim but I don't want to waste time on that. When Mr. -- when Judge Antonetti asked you about certain linguistic matters, I'm not an expert, he asked you the following: He said the official language is Bosnian, Croatian and Serbian in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he asked you whether it was a matter of language or languages. What was your answer? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember every word of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: You said that it was a matter of language, that that was the name of the language. I'm against the term "B/C/S." In Bosnia-Herzegovina we all speak the Bosnian language or the Serbian language or the Croatian language. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about three languages.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So it's not a Bosno-Croato-Serbian language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will have the break now. But before we have the break, I have a question I'd like to put to Mr. Praljak because the Judges perhaps have a procedural problem. In the course of the cross-examination on the 25th of May you intervened between 13.35 and 13.46. So you have already put questions to the witness. Why do you want to put further questions, since the rule is that once one of the parties has finished cross-examining, that's it? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, because simply some new claims have been advanced which I should like to challenge on the basis of a couple of documents, with your permission. If not, then I shall leave it for another opportunity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll see about that during the break. It's 3.30 p.m., and we will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, before we authorise you to cross-examine this witness, we'd like to know what sort of questions you'd like to put to the witness and how these questions relate to the subjects raised by the witness. We'd like to know what the relevance of these questions is. We don't want to prevent you from cross-examining the witness, but according to the rules, after the examination-in-chief there's the cross-examination, and once the cross-examination has been concluded, it's not usually possible to cross-examine again. So could you tell us something about the new issues raised and about the questions you'd like to put to this witness. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In the series of allegations made during the examination, it was said that the Bosnian army - army of Bosnia-Herzegovina - was founded on the 15th of April, 1992. I wish to demonstrate that that is not true. Twice the witness stated that the Croatian policy was hypocritical, meaning that it was duplicitous, that people meant one thing, did another, and said yet a third thing while pursuing that policy. On the basis of two documents, I wish to demonstrate what Croatia did -- had done for Bosnia and Herzegovina, in two of thousands of documents, mind you. Also, the milieu in which the Muslims -- sorry, the encirclement in which the Muslims on the east side of Mostar were after the Croato-Muslim conflict were, has been repeatedly referred to here, so I have a map here to show what extent of territory they had at their disposal and what communications -- communication links towards Jablanica and Konjic were available at the time. In addition to that, I should like to show a document about the dispatch of arms to Sarajevo which Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. -- I had sent and received a citation from the commander Zikic, the commander of the Sarajevo units, thanking us for having dispatched those weapons to them. And I do this with the intention of showing with how much enthusiasm and passion we worked on the joint front of battling the aggressor and to show the extent to which we managed despite the fact that we were unable to find the political solution to end the war conflicts within the period of a year and a half. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we decide, we believe that with regard to the issue of maps, the three dimensional one that you obtained from Google that pertains to the encirclement, we believe that that might be useful. And then there's the issue of weapons, and according to what you said, there's a document that shows that Sarajevo thanked you for your efforts. So restrict your questions to those matters, because we've discussed the issue of 15th of April a lot. And with regard to the allegations of witness about the duplicitous Croatian policies, well, this is a pure speculation. So do concentrate on the issue of the map and of the weapons, and don't forget that you have only 15 minutes. Please don't use up any more time than that. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. There is a mistake, a very important one in the transcript, I think, given your decision to allow Mr. Praljak certain questions. Page 119, line 11, it is Zikic, and it should be Vikic. A "V" is the initial, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So the name is Vikic and not Zikic. Please proceed, Mr. Praljak. You can put -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]. Thank you. Can we see the first document. Please move it a bit to the left and up. Thank you. Cross-examination by the accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Smajkic, would you please take a look at this map. On the top left it says Potoci, and the bottom right corner shows a river, and please show to Their Honours where Mostar is. Zoom in, please. Zoom in. No, no, zoom out. Zoom out. Zoom out. More, please. And more. Thank you. That's good. Mr. Smajkic, would you please point to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have the appropriate pen on you, the appropriate pointer, please use it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is Potoci here where I pointed with my pen. This is the north part from the road from Sarajevo and towards the city of Mostar. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then it goes on towards the south. This is the river Neretva?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the river Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Would you show Blagaj and the river Buna. This here is the airport. And then go down this way. This is Blagaj here. Right. And then Buna. Right.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the capital B stands for Blagaj, I expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell Their Honours, how many kilometres are there from Blagaj to Potoci?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Blagaj to Mostar it is about 12 kilometres, and then to Potoci thereabouts also; 10 kilometres or so, 12 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: We see the river Neretva here, and the left side, and not only the left side but also the right bank, in this part of Mostar was controlled after the 1993 conflict between the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO, all those parts were controlled by the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The left side of the Neretva, the left bank.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: We shall agree that from the entrance to the canyon towards Jablanica up to Blagaj there is approximately 30 kilometres. The distance between these two points is approximately 30 kilometres and there are two deep valleys there and the city of Mostar, and on the left there was a substantial part on the right part of the right bank of the Neretva which was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; am I correct in saying this?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Would you please now show the other map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just add a question? Can you show us, Witness, in which direction does the Neretva flow? Does it flow, seen on the map, from top to bottom, or the other way round?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, from top to bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can we see the next map, please. Move it a bit -- a bit up and to the left, please. Up and left. Up and left, Ms. Usher. Would you lift the map leftwards. That's it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, if you please, the arterial highway from Ploce and Metkovic, Capljina and Mostar leads towards Jablanica, Konjic and Sarajevo on the left bank of the Neretva; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: And it is controlled by the section which we just referred to, the left bank of the Neretva, under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: In that period.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Look here on the map above the G, the letter G. There is a small inlet. You can see that. An inlet above the G of the Google, of the word "Google." That's right, there. So we can see that. That is water, of course. That is a lake. That is an inlet of a lake. And across that inlet was the bridge of Bijela which, according to our information, was destroyed by Serbian artillery. Can you see from the satellite image of Google satellite image that there is a road on the left and right -- to the left and right of that inlet, a macadam road which was made when the bridge was erected and which could be used at any time to pass from Mostar towards Jablanica and Konjic? So it was an asphalt road up to the inlet point, and 150 metres there was a macadam road around the inlet, and then again an asphalt road towards Jablanica. Am I saying this correctly?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a detour there. This detour was used by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This bypass was used by it to establish contact with Jablanica after the bridge was blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Right. So we have the asphalt road Sarajevo, Konjic, Jablanica, we have this interruption of the asphalt road, we have 150 metres of macadam road, and then a continued asphalt road on towards Blagaj, Mostar and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: How, then, can we speak about the total encirclement, the total shutting off of Mostar when, in the same position as Mostar was, unfortunately, after our conflict, in the same or worse position were Sarajevo and Bihac and Zepce, Srebrenica too, and Central Bosnia, for that matter, Kiseljak, et cetera? Unfortunately, we had the situation characterised by conflicts and encirclements, but we cannot but say the truth. We have to say that the Mostar area -- we cannot say that the situation in the Mostar and its access and the roads leading outside of Mostar were such that we can speak about the severance of communications to and from Mostar; am I saying the right thing?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with you there. We can speak about that after a breakthrough, after the linking up of Mostar with Bijelo Polje, but until HVO was holding the northern camp during that period and Zalik, that was indeed a big camp. The entire city of Mostar was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can I clarify a point on the transcript? On page 123, line 13, I read we have 150 metres of a macadam road. Should it be metres or should it be kilometres? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Metres, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness -- Mr. Smajkic, I apologise, was the northern camp, was it taken by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 30th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can we then speak about this communication being free and accessible as of that date?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: So as of that date, it was open, all communication, towards Mostar with this difficult problem of 150 metres of a macadam road?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my assessment, that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we see the third document, please. Mr. Smajkic, would you be so kind as to read it out, with the dates.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Hi, Bruno. It being impossible for us to see each other and hear each other --" zoom out. Zoom out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: We can see it quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It being impossible for us to see and hear each other, I wish in this way to confirm for you receipt of MTS that you sent to my unit and to me. In addition to acknowledging receipt of the same, I also wish to profoundly thank you and to wish you and your family the best of health. Please, in addition to you, convey my gratitude to the gentlemen General Major Slobodan Praljak, to Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic, and to Minister Bozo Rajic. Bruno, in addition to these MTS that you have dispatched to me, I also require the following ..." and then he goes on to enumerate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The date, please.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 23rd of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: During this trial, there will be presented thousands of documents of this kind, but from this particular one we can see that there was a continued endeavour to help in each and every place where the aggressor wanted to or could have been successful either vis-a-vis the Muslims or the Croats or the Croats and Muslims together. Mr. Smajkic, do you think that it was very simple just to simply load these things? Do you appreciate how much effort it took, how much ability it took to load this onto trucks and have it reach Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite aware of that. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for having given me this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are requesting that these two documents be admitted into evidence. The photo isn't a problem, the document hasn't been translated into English. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to propose that it be conditionally admitted into the file and which shall, of course, ensure the necessary translation. We have asked for it to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As far as the photograph is concerned, there's no need to have it translated, but on the other hand, as far as the other document is concerned, well, we could mark it for identification. Mr. Registrar, could we have two numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, seeing that I am on my feet, I should like to tender also into evidence document 3D 00188, which I used in my cross-examination the day before yesterday, and that is a record of the hearing of the same witness in the case IT-98-34-T, from the 17th to the 19th of October, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, we need three numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The last document then mentioned by Mr. Kovacic a minute ago will therefore have the tendering date and admission date of today and will be referenced as 3D 00188. As to the two documents used by Mr. Praljak today, I understand the map will be admitted as IC document. It's going to be IC 00022. With respect to the text or the written document, we may want to admit it under IC 00023, marked for identification pending translation to be provided by Mr. Kovacic, I understand. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jonjic, try and go through a list very rapidly. Mr. Registrar, please take care, because there will be a lot of numbers now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to correct the transcript. Page 89, line 8, my question -- not the response by the witness, but my question was inserted incorrectly. This was the list of the directors of -- of elementary and secondary schools in Mostar. It seems that I suggested all were Croats and it should be quite the opposite; it should be Muslims. And now the documents. There are 18 of them, so I think it would be simpler if I say all are proceeded by a 5D mark and the first digit is 0, and then the numbers are as follows: 1104, 1105, 1106, 1107, 1108, 1109, 1110, 1111, 1112, 1113, 1091 -- 1091, 1093, 1081, 1082, 1083, 1084, 1069, and the last one, 1115. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Indeed we have a series of 18 exhibits. These are tendered and admitted with today's date: 5D 01104, 5D 01105, 5D 01106, 5D 01107, 5D 01108, 5D 01109, 5D 01110, 5D 01111, 5D 01112, 5D 01113, 5D 01091, 5D 01093, 5D 01081, 5D 01082, 5D 01083, 5D 01084, 5D 01069, 5D 01115. And this completes the list. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before I give the floor to Mr. Scott, I'd just like to comment on the number of exhibits. I'm beginning to be very concerned given the number of exhibits. I'd like to remind you that the Prosecution intended to tender 9.500 documents, but since the beginning of the trial the Defence has tendered an enormous number of documents. And with regard to Mr. Coric's documents, we have 1.115 documents. Not all have been admitted for the moment, but this means that Mr. Coric's Defence believes that they'll have more than a thousand documents to tender into evidence, and this is still the Prosecution stage. When the Defence commence, you'll have a significantly greater number of documents to tender. So we'll be dealing with more than 20.000 documents. That's quite certain. That's why I suggest that when you present your documents, when you tender your documents, be rapid, as Mr. Jonjic was, and we'll then be able to admit documents into evidence more easily. We're following this very closely, and naturally we'll examine everything in detail under a magnifying glass. We have now reached the stage of re-examination. Mr. Scott, let me remind you that re-examination must relate to the questions put in the course of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Before I begin, Your Honour, just an observation, and I'm not really casting stones at the Defence because I think everyone in this institution realises the difficulty of translation - I'm not talking about interpretation in the courtroom but the translation of documents - can be. Having said that, a substantial number of Defence documents have not been translated, and of course that makes it virtually impossible for the Prosecution and presumably for most of the Judges to make much sense of these documents or to ask informed questions on the documents when they've not yet been translated, and then the witness of course is gone, and it's very impossible to really deal with the documents adequately in that way. Having said that, Your Honour, my questions to Mufti Smajkic are primarily in the nature of things that he indicated during cross-examination he wanted to clarify and add comments to, and he was repeatedly told during the cross-examination that the Prosecution could give him the opportunity to clarify those matters or address those matters. So based on that, I do indeed want to give him the opportunity to clarify a number of things, but all arising from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The first of those, Mufti Smajkic, is this: You talked about in direct examination -- or it came up perhaps in cross-examination, excuse me, the appointment of Mr. Jaganjac as the commander of the unified Croat-Muslim forces in connection with the defence for liberation of Mostar. I believe you said in response to Defence question from Mr. Stojic's counsel, most of these people -- excuse me. Most people thought that Mr. Jaganjac's appointment would be helpful, would be a conciliatory gesture, but I want to give you the chance to say did it in fact turn out at that way? Was -- that may have been the intention. What happened in reality?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I actually stated, and I had a lot of friends and relatives who were in a dilemma. They didn't know whether to join the HVO - and this is the truth - because if they did so, they would have weapons and certain other benefits. However, if they remained in the army, they wouldn't have any weapons, and they wouldn't have everything they would have been provided with had they been in the HVO. What they were concerned with was focusing their efforts on defeating a common enemy. This is why they thought in this way. So they thought, well, they're finally sending us someone from Croatia who was in the Croatian army, at the same time he's a Muslim, so it was a form of reconciliation. That's what people wanted. But I can't really criticise Mr. Jaganjac because he was just carrying out orders. He had a command that was above him. But I'm firmly convinced that this was done to attract armed individuals who might be able to contribute to liberating that territory. They wanted to ensure that they joined the HVO and that, as a result, the armija would be weakened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You also -- it was also pointed out to you in cross-examination that when the Mostar Crisis Staff was disbanded on about the 15th of May, 1992, and these separate or new structures, HVO structures, were put into place, it was pointed out to you on a number of documents that some persons who were Muslims were put in various of these positions, and I believe you attempted to say in answer to some questions about this that most of the -- how -- despite the fact that they were originally put in those positions, that they did not remain in those positions very long, but I want to give you a further opportunity to address that. How was that the case, and explain that to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott, for that question. That's true. I felt very uneasy when Ms. Nozica showed me that document, and I quite simply had to react because that's correct. That is true. There were -- 50 per cent of the staff were Muslims, and there were that many Croats. And Commander Jaganjac was a Muslim, or he was a member of the Muslim Corps. However, our people, the Muslims who were present in that area at the time, had to face incredible problems in that there were disavowals of everything that resembled the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There's no doubt about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to such an answer because the witness is talking about other people's experiences and the situation they found themselves in and how they reacted to that situation. I think that the witness can testify about what he has personal knowledge about, and if the Prosecution believes that it's necessary to provide further arguments, they can use other witnesses to demonstrate or to prove the sort of situation they were in. The witness cannot comment on such things. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but may I add something, Ms. Nozica. These gentlemen brought copies of resignations from these positions. Apart from the resignation of Mr. Hadziosmanovic, they provided me with such copies. I'm not inventing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you know -- I'm not asking you to speculate, but based on what you've just said, if you know, why were the Muslims who were initially named to some of these positions by the HVO, why were they resigning from these positions?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They resigned for the simple reason that anti-Bosnian policies were being pursued. What was at stake was implementing a programme achieving objectives established on the 18th of November, 1991, and that objective was the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. I'm going to move forward, because I don't want to take too much additional time this afternoon, to the question of your appointment -- or recommendation, I should say, of this man who became a cleric in the Muslim forces in the Mostar area. And I want to make sure that's as clear as possible. And it may assist if the registry could please show the witness -- or please display Exhibit 2D 00013. And while that's being done, to remind you, Mufti Smajkic, and the courtroom what was said in particular about this, Mr. Kovacic read to you -- put this question to you: "Mr. Arif Pasalic or someone --" this is at page 2634 of the transcript. "Mr. Arif Pasalic or someone else asked me who would be responsible for the appointment. I then contacted some people in Zenica as well as Mr. Mahmut Rajlic [phoen], who was the commander --" and then the interpreters corrected that, not the commander but who was the Emir of the 7th Brigade. If you recall those questions and answers with Mr. Kovacic. Now, if you look -- if you have now in front of you 2D 00013. I just want to make sure there is no confusion in the courtroom. The person that you appointed to this clerical position, this was someone in the Mostar Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.
